go-embedded-r/r is BSD-3-Clause and the R code of base R is GPL-2-or-later, so the rule is: base R’s R code is rewritten, never copied. A rule that depends on what a contributor (human or model) remembers is not enough. In v0.12.0, eval/baselib/datetime.R was written from the help pages but partly from memory of R’s code, and came out close to R’s text. It was rewritten in v0.12.2 (pull request 30), and cmd/cleanroom now checks every file of eval/baselib against the R library code of R 4.6.2.
The gate is a floor, not proof. It bounds accidents and careless restructuring. A short function has one natural spelling, so a tiny file can be a copy and pass, and the checker cannot see a rewrite from memory that happens to differ. The provenance record below is the other half, and the gate does not replace the rule.

data.provenance-in-every-pull-request#Provena: .github/pull_request_template.md asks, for any change under eval/baselib/: the .Rd pages read, whether any R function body was seen and how (and who then rewrote the file blind), and the gate score of the first draft before any reshaping. Pull request 30 records its own provenance: datetime.R and vectors.R were rewritten by the agent that built the gate, which saw only the checker’s references and scores; conditions.R was rewritten blind by a separate agent, after the first rewrite was replaced because its author had read the old 10-line file; that agent saw one base closure’s printed body when the oracle printed it, which is why the guard exists.

data.the-oracle-guard#The oracle guard:
Printing a base function in the reference R shows its GPL body, and this happened once while checking a behaviour. internal/oracle/oracle.R therefore refuses, with the error oracle: printing base closures is disallowed by the clean-room rule, to print, deparse, dput, body, as.list, format, serialize or return any closure of base, stats, utils, methods and the other packages of R, however it is reached (auto-print, :::, getAnywhere, inside a list or an attribute, or a copy made in the global environment, recognised with identical() against the bodies and formals of every function of those packages, at any size, including copies made with body<-, attr<- or as.function). .Internal is refused in requests. Closures of our own print, and goldens that compare function printing use closures defined in the snippet.
Until v0.12.3 a base closure whose body was under 100 serialized bytes could be copied out of the namespace and printed (issue 31, closed by pull request 32); the size floor is gone. Someone with an installed R can still read its sources, which is why the rule is procedural too.
data.the-similarity-checker#The similarity ch: Method. Our own lexer (package syntax) cuts both files into tokens, comments dropped. K-grams of tokens are hashed and thinned by winnowing (Schleimer, Wilkerson and Aiken, Winnowing: Local Algorithms for Document Fingerprinting, SIGMOD 2003: the minimum hash of each window, the rightmost on a tie; any shared run of k+w-1 tokens shares a fingerprint, and no run shorter than k can). Parameters: k = 8, w = 4. Two views. Identifiers kept (exact), and every identifier replaced by one placeholder (normalised, which sees a renamed copy). The score is containment: the share of our fingerprints found in one R file. The longest common token run is reported with file:line on both sides. Runs count code tokens only (literals and commas do not, so a table of month names is not a copy). Formal argument lists are excluded. function( up to the matching ), defaults included, is not fingerprinted in either view: a help page fixes the signature, so independent code must repeat it. R’s sources are read, never stored. The checker reads src/library/*/R/*.R of an R 4.6.2 tree at check time (RGO_RSOURCE, or --rsrc) and prints only references (file:line), never R’s text. The gate runs in CI. The oracle lane downloads the tarball by SHA-256 and runs the gate there (RGO_REQUIRE_RSOURCE=1: the gate must run, not skip). It also runs as a Go test, which skips without R’s sources.

data.known-divergences#Known divergences:
Both are platform effects, not semantics.
exp10. Numeric constants with a decimal exponent beyond about 200 in magnitude: R takes a power of ten from the C library’s exp10, which on macOS is not always the correctly rounded value. 5 of 100 000 random literals of that kind (1e229, 1e303, 1e-244) deparse with one more digit in Go (1.00000000000000e+229). No such constant occurs in R’s sources or tests. x86-64 long double. On x86-64 Linux, where R parses and formats numbers in 80-bit long double with its own digits routine, 6 of the 90 files of R’s tests/ deparse with a different last digit in some constant (1e-270 against 9.99999999999999e-271, -5152.07935578853 against ...52). The CI lane on Linux reports that verdict and gates the other three columns and all of src/library.
data.parity-with-r-462#Parity with R 4.6.2:
Judged by the oracle: the same input is parsed, then deparsed by R and by Go, for deparse() and print().
Corpus Inputs Deparse R src/library: every .R file of the base packages (7.8 MB) 844 (842 parse, 2 rejected) 842 / 842 R tests/: 95 files (1 is not UTF-8 and is skipped) 94 (90 parse, 4 rejected) 90 / 90 our snippets 42 42 / 42 our deparse cases (parentheses, precedence, line breaking, indentation, constants, names) 65 (2 rejected) 63 / 63 differential fuzz: 610 000 random edits of lines of R’s sources 610 000 all decimal literals, random (up to 20 digits, exponents -330..330) 100 000 99 995 identical, 5 not The complete table, with the tree, token and error columns, is on The parser.
data.what-it-is-written-from#What it is writt: Deparse is written from the documented behaviour of deparse(): precedence and parenthesisation, the 60-byte line cutoff with its break points and indentation, if/else layout inside braces, structure-free constants, 15-significant-digit numbers, and string escapes with R’s own table of printable characters. That table is generated by the oracle into syntax/print_gen.go, and the list of primitives that deparse as function calls into syntax/prims_gen.go. No R source is copied.

The package is github.com/go-embedded-r/r/eval, in v0.28.0 (bounded by default since v0.4.0).
s := eval.NewSession(eval.Options{}) // bounded by default since v0.4.0 res, err := s.Eval("f <- function(x, y = 2) x * y; f(21)") // one notebook cell res, err = s.EvalContext(ctx, src) // the same, cancellable res.Value, res.Visible // the last value, whether R would print it res.Output, res.Stderr // what print/cat and the auto-print wrote; message() output res.Warnings // []eval.Warning{Message, Call} // err is *eval.Error{Message, Call, Condition, Output, Stderr, Warnings} (R's own text), // *syntax.Error or *syntax.LimitError; a timeout or a cancel unwraps to context.DeadlineExceeded / Canceled s.Get("x"); s.Set("x", v) // the global environment persists from one cell to the next
data.evaluating#Evaluating: Eval(src) parses the source and evaluates its expressions in order in the global environment, as one notebook cell. The result is that of the last one. EvalContext(ctx, src) is the same, and ends with an *eval.Error wrapping the context’s error when ctx is done. EvalIn(ctx, src, env) is EvalContext in the given environment, a child of the global one for a cell that must not leave names behind. Get(name) and Set(name, v) read and write the global environment.
data.limits-bounded-by-default#Limits: bounde:
Since v0.4.0 the zero eval.Options{} is bounded. This is a breaking change: before it, MaxSteps, MaxAlloc and Timeout were unbounded unless set. A zero field now selects its default:
Option Meaning Default MaxSteps calls and loop iterations evaluated by one Eval 30 000 000 MaxAlloc bytes of vector storage allocated in total by one Eval, copies included 16 GiB Timeout time one Eval may take; a context given to EvalContext bounds it too 10 s MaxDepth nesting of evaluations (R’s expressions); beyond it, evaluation nested too deeply. Since v0.17.1 it also bounds the recursion of every native that walks the structure of a value (identical, printing, format, deparse, substitute, unlist, anyNA, cat, recursive [[<-, saveRDS and readRDS, language objects), on one shared counter per session 5000 (DefaultMaxDepth); 300 under GOOS=js and GOOS=wasip1 MaxVector length of any vector the runtime allocates 2^28 elements Parse a syntax.Limits bounding the source text of an Eval see syntax.Limits MaxFileBytes (v0.13.0) the in-memory file system, any one file read or written under FileRoot, and what a text connection holds 256 MiB (DefaultMaxFileBytes); eval.Unbounded removes it FileRoot (v0.13.0) a host directory as the session’s file-system root, confined with os.OpenRoot empty: a private in-memory tree the host never sees; Session.Close releases a root Env (v0.13.0) the environment variables the session sees through Sys.getenv nil: empty; the host’s environment is never read Past MaxDepth, R’s own errors are raised and the session stays usable: CStackOverflowError (C stack usage N is too close to the limit) for deep data and expressionStackOverflowError (evaluation nested too deeply: infinite recursion / options(expressions=)?) for deep calls; both inherit stackOverflowError. Under GOOS=js and GOOS=wasip1 the default is 300, because a WebAssembly engine’s own stack, which Go cannot grow, overflows with a JS RangeError that kills the instance (measured with node and V8’s default 984 KB stack: 2 548 nested R calls, 10 419 levels of data in identical); a host that knows its stack is larger sets Options.MaxDepth.
The file-system and environment options are described, with the security properties they give an embedder, on Files and connections.
The first three defaults were measured, not guessed (RGO_MEASURE=1 go test -run TestMeasureLimits -v ./eval): the 1 035 goldens of v0.5.0 need at most 8 879 steps, 0.8 MB and 3 ms, and the heaviest cells a notebook runs on purpose (a loop of 10^6 iterations: 3 million steps, 0.17 s; a list grown by 20 000 assignments: 1.6 GB of copies, 0.63 s) set the scale. Each default is about ten times that.
A limit that is hit ends the evaluation with an R error that names it and leaves the session usable.
Opting out is explicit. To remove a limit, say so: MaxSteps: eval.Unbounded (also for MaxAlloc and Timeout; eval.Unbounded is -1). A zero never means unbounded, and any other negative value panics in NewSession. Use Unbounded only for trusted code. A context given to EvalContext still stops an unbounded session.
The bomb tests (while (TRUE) 0, numeric(1e12), 1:1e12, unbounded recursion, an allocation loop) assert a refusal under a Go memory limit, and in CI under ulimit -v.
data.maxalloc-is-a-budget-not-live-memory#Max: MaxAlloc counts every byte of vector storage one Eval allocates, copies included, over the whole evaluation. It is a cumulative budget, not the memory alive at any moment: a cell can stay far below 16 GiB resident and still spend it. The 16 GiB default is sized for a native process. An embedder with little memory, such as a WebAssembly one, should set MaxAlloc much lower.
data.result-and-errors#Result and errors:
Result carries Value, Visible, Output (what print() and cat() wrote, and the auto-printed value of every visible top-level expression, as an R console shows them), Stderr (message() output) and Warnings (the warnings raised and not muffled, each with its message and call).
An error is an *eval.Error with Message (R’s conditionMessage), Call (the deparsed conditionCall, empty for none), Condition (the condition object that was signalled; nil for limits and interrupts), and the Output, Stderr and Warnings the cell had produced before it failed. Its text is R’s: Error in f(1) : object 'y' not found. A parse failure is a *syntax.Error or a *syntax.LimitError.
data.session#Session:
NewSession(Options) makes one interpreter: a global environment that persists from one Eval to the next, so names assigned by one cell are seen by the next.
A Session is not safe for concurrent use. Cells run one at a time; an embedder that serves several callers uses one session per caller, or serialises the calls itself.

Slice 10 (M3, v0.13.0 and v0.13.1) adds connections and files, documented on Files and connections.
Slice 9 (M3, v0.12.0 and v0.12.1) adds dates and times. Classes: Date, POSIXct, POSIXlt (a list of the 11 components with tzone and balanced), difftime. Functions: Sys.time, Sys.Date, as.Date, as.POSIXct, as.POSIXlt (character with format and tryFormats, numeric with origin, Date, between classes, factors), strptime (every conversion R’s help page lists, %OS, %z, 24:00, names matched without case, trailing text ignored), format/strftime/as.character (usetz, digits, %OSn, options(digits.secs)), ISOdate, ISOdatetime, weekdays, months, quarters, julian, difftime, as.difftime, units, units<-, format and print of differences, seq.Date (day, week, month, quarter, year, a number, a difftime), c, [, [[, [<-, rep, rev, sort, unique, mean, range, diff on all three classes, arithmetic, comparisons and Math/Summary of difftime with R’s rules. Non-finite times are kept apart as R 4.2 does. Time zones come from Go’s embedded IANA database (time/tzdata, about 450 KB in the binary): tz = "" is the session’s zone, the TZ variable else the system’s (the oracle runs with TZ=UTC and so do the goldens); a repeated local hour reads as its first occurrence, as R’s does. Support added on the way: options, getOption, deparse1, gettext, gettextf, rep.int, is.factor, pmatch, unname; as.character and paste of a factor give its labels; print forwards its arguments to the method; deparse writes attributes as structure(...). Slice 8 (M3, v0.11.0) adds environments and a one-namespace model. Bindings: lockBinding, unlockBinding, bindingIsLocked, lockEnvironment(bindings =), environmentIsLocked, makeActiveBinding, bindingIsActive, activeBindingFunction, delayedAssign; every assignment (<-, <<-, assign, $<-, [[<-, list2env, replacement forms) honours locks and runs active bindings, with R’s messages and calls; the base environment and all its bindings are locked as in R (assign("sum", 1, baseenv()) is refused). rm takes inherits; get/get0/exists/mget take mode, inherits and ifnotfound and give R’s messages; exists does not force a promise. as.list is generic (as.list.environment with all.names and sorted, .default, .function, .factor); eapply, with, within (lists), withVisible, names(env). data.design-choices#Design choices: Clean room. R’s C code is a specification, never a source. The design is written from the R Language Definition, R Internals, the help pages and what the oracle (GNU R 4.6.2) does; each slice is checked by the oracle lane before it is merged. Bounded. Recursion depth (R’s own expressions limit, 5000), vector allocation size and evaluation steps are session limits, refused with R’s own error, never a Go crash. Typed Go slices for vectors, not []interface{}: arithmetic loops run over []float64 and []int32, and NA is a value inside the slice (R’s INT_MIN and NaN-payload conventions), never a side bitmap. Calls are *Lang with an argument slice, not pairlists; a real pairlist type is only for formals, attributes and pairlist(). Attributes are an ordered slice, because their order is observable. Symbols are interned, so quote(x) == quote(x) is pointer equality. *Missing is its own type, for f(x, ) and missing(). No byte-code: the AST walker is the semantics; a faster tier would be a later, measured decision. Closures take promises: lazy arguments, missing, ..., with R’s three-pass argument matching (exact name, unique partial name, position). Lexical control flow is not panic-based on the hot path (break, next, return travel as a flow code); errors and non-lexical exits use a typed Go panic recovered at the owning context. Conditions: handlers are a stack on the session. Exiting handlers unwind with a typed panic caught by their tryCatch, calling handlers run with the stack truncated below them, and restarts are found by name. Errors are signalled as conditions before they end the evaluation, so tryCatch(error=) and withCallingHandlers(error=) see them. Replacement functions use always-copy semantics; the ownership optimisation stays deferred. The oracle judges. Goldens are R’s answers to inputs written in the repository, compared byte for byte; the tests replay them without R.

Of slice 9 (v0.12.0 and v0.12.1):
The C locale only (English names, %x is %m/%d/%y, %c the C form; %E and %O modifiers read as the plain conversion). R’s warning datetimes before 1902 may not be accurate (once per session) is never given. The daylight abbreviation in the tzone attribute of a zone with unusual or no daylight time is found by scanning Go’s transitions and differs from R’s for some zones (56 of 445 fuzz cases: the attribute has three elements, the first is always right). Of the local times that a daylight-saving change skips or repeats, ours read as R’s in most cases, and 64 of 478 fuzz cases differ. %s is not the epoch time on macOS: R gives the fields read as UTC unless the format also has %z or %Z, in which case it subtracts the zone’s offset. That is reproduced exactly (the 9 goldens of platform_darwin.R, the fuzz). Whether glibc does the same is not known, so those goldens are not compared on Linux. The call shown in an error from a long structure(...) breaks its lines where R does not. Date and POSIXct have no round, trunc, cut, summary, seq.POSIXt, Sys.setenv, Sys.timezone, OlsonNames, and date columns in data frames were not checked in v0.17.0. Of slice 8 (v0.11.0):
There is no package loading: no library, require, loadNamespace, attach, search, sys.source (planned with the slices that need them). The installed packages other than base (stats, utils, …) resolve through our base environment (utils::head works, stats::sd is “‘sd’ is not an exported object”), and any other name is there is no package called ‘x’. parent.env(globalenv()) is base; R’s is the last attached package. as.list.environment and names(env) list in creation order, where R’s hashed order is unspecified. sys.call() and parent.frame() inside eval/local do not see R’s eval frame. The text requireNamespace("foo") writes without quiet was read from the oracle, not goldened (its harness adds a connection warning). print of an environment does not list its attributes. getNamespace() raises R’s message with another call. within has no data frame method. Of slice 7 (v0.10.0), all because R runs tryCatch and try through closures we do not have:
the conditionCall of a stop() made directly inside try() or tryCatch() at top level is empty here, and R’s internal call there (doTryCatch(...), try(...)); match.call(expand.dots = FALSE) keeps ... as a list where R keeps a pairlist (deparse shows list( for pairlist(); absolute frame numbers differ from the oracle’s, which runs each snippet inside its own harness frames, so the goldens compare numbers of frames relative to a starting point; computeRestarts has no top-level abort restart. Of slice 5 (v0.8.0):
A matrix whose dimnames carry names (names(dimnames(x)), as table() makes) prints without the variable-name header lines R adds. lgamma, digamma and trigamma are less accurate than R’s: an open defect, issue 14; the fuzz compares them through signif(x, 12) and counts them. mean sums in float64 (with R’s second pass) where R uses long double: last-bit differences are possible on long sums. The math fuzz compares libm functions within 4 ulp (largest seen: 2), not exactly: the last bit of those functions depends on the C library. Of slice 3:
Regular expressions: TRE’s approximate-matching syntax is not ported, non-ASCII classes use Go’s Unicode tables, perl = TRUE is refused, and grepl is 1.44 times slower than R (an open defect); see Regular expressions. sort of non-atomic values is not implemented. Collation (decided in slice 4): strings sort and compare as R 4.6.2 does under the oracle’s C.UTF-8, which is ICU order, not code point (punctuation, digits, letters; accents after the plain letter; lowercase before uppercase). Strings outside Latin script compare by code point after the Latin letters, a documented divergence. See M3 plan / base coverage. Widths of sprintf and format above 2^24 are refused. sprintf("%05d", NA) zero-pads the NA as macOS does, where glibc pads with spaces (the C library decides in R, so the golden leaves it out). From the platform rather than the semantics:
The bits of a NaN (its sign, whether it is quiet) are whatever the hardware made of it, so goldens and the fuzz compare NA against NaN, not their payloads. exp and the power with a fractional or negative exponent can differ from the C library’s pow/exp in the last bit (the fuzz keeps the exponents integral and leaves exp out; they come with go-numerics in M4). The 2 of 190 000 arithmetic fuzz cases are one of each (a pow last bit, and NA %% 3 added to a NaN). min/max of a character vector mixed with numbers is not collated like R’s. The modulus family is written with explicit fused multiply-adds, as R is compiled on arm64, so it gives the same result everywhere; R on x86-64 Linux does not fuse, so its %% of huge doubles can differ there (the CI lane reports the evaluator fuzz on Linux, it does not gate it).

rawConnection (modes r, w, a, rb, wb, ab) and rawConnectionValue read and write a raw vector in memory. readBin reads integers (1, 2, 4 and 8 bytes, signed or not), doubles (4 and 8), logicals, complex numbers, raw vectors and character strings, with endian; writeBin is its inverse; readChar and writeChar work on characters, seek and isSeekable on positions. All of them take a raw vector, a file name, a file connection or a raw connection, and obey the same MaxFileBytes bound as the other connections.
Every allocation is checked before it is made: readBin(n = 1e12), raw(1e12), rawToBits(raw(2^26)) and writeChar(nchars = 1e12) are refused, and readBin allocates by the bytes there are, not by n. A decoder fuzz (FuzzReadBin, 900 000 executions) found no crash.

data.security-what-an-embedder-can-rely-on#Se:
These are properties of every eval.Session, tested and not just intended.
The file system is private by default. A session has an in-memory tree that the host never sees and that no other session shares. R code running in it cannot read or write a host file, and the cell’s getwd(), tempfile() and list.files() all stay inside the tree.
Options.FileRoot is the only way to reach the host’s disk, and it is confined. It gives the session a host directory as its root, opened with Go’s os.OpenRoot (os.Root). Tests cover:
.. (it is clamped at the root); absolute paths (they are read as relative to the root); symbolic links that point out of the root (they cannot leave it); a symbolic-link swap race (a path swapped for a link between the check and the use); Windows path forms. Session.Close releases the root. Do not point FileRoot at a directory that holds anything the cell must not read: the confinement is to that directory, not inside it.
The host’s environment is never read. Sys.getenv reads a table of the session’s own, Options.Env; nil means empty. Sys.setenv and Sys.unsetenv change that table only.
Everything is bounded.
Bound Value Options.MaxFileBytes default DefaultMaxFileBytes, 256 MiB (eval.Unbounded removes it): the in-memory file system, any one file read or written under FileRoot, and what a text connection holds; past it the call fails with the file size limit of this session was reached entries in the in-memory tree 65 536 path length 4 096 bytes (v0.13.1) path depth 256 levels (v0.13.1) open connections 128 sinks 20 readRDS refuses a document that expands past the limit (gzip bombs) sink output and capture.output bounded; diverted output never reaches the Result Sys.sleep obeys Timeout and the context The bomb and boundary tests (eval/io_test.go) assert these refusals under a memory limit.

go-embedded-r/r is BSD-3-Clause (see its LICENSE). The sources of R are GPL-2-or-later, so:
R is an oracle, never a source. R is run as a black box and what it prints is recorded. No R source file, no R test file, no R help page, no .Rout.save transcript and no text of R’s manuals is copied into the repository, and none is downloaded at run time. The golden files are the answers of R 4.6.2 to inputs written there. Base R’s R code is rewritten, not copied. The R-language parts of the base packages (base, stats, utils, methods, …) will be re-implemented under the BSD licence from the documented behaviour and from what the oracle does. Fetching the GPL code on first use, and a GPL port, were considered and rejected (decision of 2026-11-01, recorded in the roadmap). Contributors work from specifications: the R Language Definition, the R Internals manual, the help pages, and the oracle’s behaviour. Do not open src/main, src/nmath or the R code of the base packages while writing the counterpart. See CONTRIBUTING.md and NOTICE. data.collation-decided-in-slice-4#Collation (: R 4.6.2 started with LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 (the oracle’s locale) still orders strings with ICU, not by code point: sort(c("b", "A", "a", "B")) is "a" "A" "b" "B", punctuation sorts before digits before letters, and accents come after the plain letter. data.how-it-is-measured#How it is measured: testdata/base/exports.tsv: the 1 362 functions exported by base, with their kind (primitive or closure), generated by the oracle (R 4.6.2) and regenerated when R is bumped. testdata/base/needs.tsv: for each closure, the names of the .Internal functions it calls; internals.tsv: per internal, the number of call sites and of closures. data.shared-engines-decided-2026-11-10-and-20:
go-embedded-r does not write its own copy of an engine that several languages of the fleet need (go-embedded-ruby/ruby#918). It binds the shared library and keeps only a thin layer that is faithful to GNU R: call shapes, argument defaults, the result lists, the messages.
Numerics (M4, stats): optim, optimize, uniroot, nlm, nlminb, nls, integrate, ODE solvers, and the special functions (gamma, beta, besselJ and the rest) bind go-numerics. Where GNU R’s algorithm differs from go-numerics’ default, the R layer selects R’s (for example optim’s Nelder–Mead constants, uniroot’s tolerance rule, integrate’s QUADPACK routine) and records in its divergences when a result is not bit-identical to GNU R’s. go-numerics now states an accuracy contract: a bound on the error against an extended-precision oracle (math/big or mpmath), see go-numerics optimize#61 and special#69. When a result is not bit-identical to GNU R’s, the R layer quotes that bound as the guarantee instead of calling the difference “last-bit noise”; bit-exact arithmetic stays an option. Statistics (descriptive statistics, tests, the distributions): bind go-statistics/stats (v0.1.1 since slice 19), and later go-statistics/models for lm, glm and anova; not go-numerics, which has no statistics kernel. The R layer keeps the glue (NA, na.rm, use=, names, recycling) and binds a function only where go-statistics meets the bound this repository states against math/big (the test is in eval/stats18_bind_test.go); where it does not, the kernel stays here and the gap is listed in the README, for the owner of go-statistics to close. The upstream gaps are go-statistics/stats#24, #25, #26 and #27. What R does better goes upstream. When R’s reference has an algorithm, a default or a test problem that go-numerics lacks, it is added to go-numerics for the whole fleet, not to the R layer. This applies only to what is available outside R’s own GPL text: published papers and netlib’s public domain or BSD code (QUADPACK, MINPACK, PORT). R’s own C and R sources, nmath included, stay unread here and are never ported into a shared library. Linear algebra: slice 13, done in slice 20 (v0.22.0) on go-ndarray v0.44.0’s linalg. What it lacks (LU factors, a condition estimator, a pivoted QR, dqrdc2, dormqr, dtrtrs, a pivoted Cholesky) is written here and listed in the README as gaps for its owner. Regex perl = TRUE: go-regexp/pcre2. Compression (gzfile, memCompress): the shared zlib. Random numbers (M4): the shared bit generators, as long as their state reads back as R’s .Random.seed. Files, environment, clock: go-embedded-r has the no-host mode (the default in-memory tree) and the confined-root mode (Options.FileRoot) since v0.13.0. It adopts the shared host and sandbox layer (go-embedded-julia/julia#32) when that layer has both modes.

data.3-randomseed-compatibility#3. .Random.se:
R 3.6.0 and later default to RNGkind("Mersenne-Twister", "Inversion", "Rejection") (?RNGkind). The facts below come from ?RNGkind, ?sample and ?Normal; everything the pages leave open is pinned by an oracle experiment before the code is written.
Mersenne-Twister: Matsumoto & Nishimura (1998), “code updated in 2002”. The tempering and the 624-word recurrence are the published algorithm, which go-ndarray’s MT19937.Uint32 already implements (random/mt19937.go:108-136). The seed vector: .Random.seed is 626 integers: element 1 codes the kinds (units and tens: the uniform kind; hundreds: the normal kind; ten-thousands: the sample kind), element 2 is the position in the state, elements 3–626 are the 624 words, read as unsigned (so they can be negative or NA in R). Our .Random.seed is a plain integer vector in the global environment; reading it calls State(), assigning it calls SetState after validation. set.seed: R uses “its own initialization method due to B. D. Ripley” (?RNGkind), not Matsumoto–Nishimura’s init_genrand and not NumPy’s legacy seeding (SeedLegacy). The method is pinned by experiment: set.seed(s) for a few hundred s (0, 1, negative, .Machine$integer.max, NA), with .Random.seed dumped after each, is the golden; the scrambling is then written to reproduce the 626 integers exactly. The uniform map: ?RNGkind says the generators “return 32-bit integer values that are converted to doubles”, and ?Uniform that runif never returns 0 or 1. The exact map (scaling constant, the guard at the ends) is pinned by drawing after set.seed and comparing each double with the 32-bit word read from .Random.seed. Inversion: rnorm applies the normal quantile to uniform draws (?RNGkind refers to ?qnorm: Wichura 1988, AS 241). How many 32-bit words each normal consumes is read from the change of .Random.seed[2] across rnorm(1), not assumed. The quantile is go-statistics’ Normal.PPF (≤ 0.55 ulp); where R’s AS 241 is farther from mpmath than ours, the value differs in the last bit and the golden counts it. Rejection: sample.kind = "Rejection" (R 3.6.0, PR#17494) replaced “Rounding”. The number of words drawn per index, and the rejection rule, are pinned the same way, from .Random.seed[2], for n just below and above powers of two and for n ≥ 2^31 (“two random numbers are used”, ?sample). “Rounding” is kept for RNGversion("3.5.0"). Walker alias and sequential sampling without replacement (?sample), from Ripley (1987). Other kinds: Wichmann-Hill, Marsaglia-Multicarry, Super-Duper, Knuth-TAOCP(-2002), L’Ecuyer-CMRG and Box-Muller / Kinderman-Ramage / Ahrens-Dieter are refused with eval.Unsupported in slice 24 and added later from their papers, in demand order; ?RNGkind’s description of each (for example the Wichmann-Hill multipliers and moduli) is the starting point. Gates: the goldens compare the whole .Random.seed after each call, not only the values; a differential fuzz mode runs random sequences of set.seed, runif, sample, rnorm and RNGkind against the oracle and compares the state after each.
data.4-upstream-gaps-pull-requests-coordinate:
Each gap goes to its library as a pull request, agreed beforehand with that organisation’s owners. Nothing is written into their trackers from this repository. Until a gap lands, the R function it serves is eval.Unsupported (never a local approximation that would need replacing).
go-ndarray/ndarray (random):
MT19937.SetState stores Pos without checking it (random/mt19937.go:159-162); a position above 624 makes the next Uint32 index past the state. R lets a user assign any .Random.seed, so either the setter validates, or the R layer does. The R layer validates in slice 24 in any case; the PR adds the check where every binding benefits. go-numerics/special (its docs/roadmap.md, 2026-11-11, lists these):
the log-space set (Log1mExp, LogAddExp, LogSubExp, Log1pmx), LogGamma1p, SinPi/CosPi/TanPi (items 1, 3, 4): the log.p and lower.tail paths of slices 26–27; Stirlerr, Bd0 and the raw binomial/Poisson densities, today private in go-statistics (item 2): the saddle-point densities (Loader 2000, cited by ?Binomial, ?Poisson, ?GammaDist); log-probability inverses for GammaPInv and BetaIncInv (item A1): qgamma, qbeta with log.p = TRUE; and a bound for BetaIncInv at a or b < 1e-3 (go-numerics/special#11), which qbeta reaches; noncentral beta, t and F, Owen’s T (items 5, 10): Lenth (1987) AS 226 and Frick (1990), Lenth (1989) AS 243, as ?Beta, ?TDist and ?FDist cite them; Tukey studentized range and the exact Wilcoxon and signed-rank distributions (item 11; the roadmap leaves open whether they belong in go-statistics): Copenhaver & Holland (1988) and Odeh & Evans AS 70 (?Tukey); the accuracy outliers that slice 25 lists as divergences: logbeta near log B = 0, digamma near its negative roots, jv at half-integer order. go-statistics/stats:
d/p/q for the families of slice 27 that it lacks (noncentral t, beta and F; Tukey; Wilcoxon; signed rank), on top of special’s items above; samplers over a uniform source, separate from the NumPy-compatible Rvs, implementing the algorithms R documents: Kachitvichyanukul & Schmeiser (1988) for the binomial, Ahrens & Dieter (1982, TOMS 8(2)) for Poisson, Ahrens & Dieter (1982, CACM 25(1)) and (1974) for gamma, Cheng (1978) for beta, Kachitvichyanukul & Schmeiser (1985) for the hypergeometric, Ahrens & Dieter (1972) for the exponential, Devroye (1986) for the negative binomial and geometric; quantiles at a log probability (PPF from LogCDF/LogSF); its dependencies are old (special v0.5.3, optimize v0.6.0 in its go.mod): a bump to special ≥ v0.20 and optimize ≥ v0.9 comes first, so the r module does not carry two versions’ accuracy. go-numerics/optimize (its docs/roadmap.md already plans the first two):
PORT nlminb from netlib (roadmap item 7; netlib licence notice to be checked first, as the roadmap says); extendInt-style bracket extension (roadmap D2); R’s optim variants, which are not SciPy’s: Nelder-Mead with alpha 1.0, beta 0.5, gamma 2.0, and BFGS and CG “based originally on Pascal code in Nash (1990)” (?optim), CG type 1–3 (Fletcher-Reeves, Polak-Ribière, Beale-Sorenson); implemented from Nash’s book, the code’s licence checked before any is read; SANN (Bélisle 1992, ?optim); nlm’s method: Dennis & Schnabel (1983) and Schnabel, Koontz & Weiss (1985), cited by ?nlm; polyroot: no polynomial root finder exists in go-numerics or go-ndarray (searched in the module cache); Jenkins & Traub (1972) Algorithm 419 (?polyroot). The repository is agreed with the owners. go-numerics/integrate:
a batched (vector) integrand for Quad: today Quad takes func(float64) float64, while R calls f once per rule application with all its nodes (?integrate: “f must accept a vector of inputs”); the number and order of f’s calls is observable in R. This is part of integrate’s roadmap item 4 (batched calls).
data.5-gates-per-slice#5. Gates, per slice:
The five gates of M3 (goldens, differential fuzz with exclusions counted, FuzzEval, bomb tests under GOMEMLIMIT, performance) apply, plus:
every numeric golden records our error and R’s error against the oracle (mpmath, math/big), and fails when ours exceeds the slice’s bound; bomb tests for the new resource paths: sample.int(1e15, 1e9), rnorm(2^31), integrate with subdivisions = 1e9, optim with maxit = .Machine$integer.max all refuse under eval.Options limits; the coverage metric of M3 extends to stats (rparity gains a statscov mode on the oracle’s ls("package:stats")).
data.clean-room-unchanged-from-m3#Clean room: Specification: R’s help pages (rendered from the .Rd files by the oracle) and the observed behaviour of the oracle (R 4.6.2, through internal/oracle). R’s .R and .c files, src/nmath included, are never read. Algorithms: from the papers that the help pages cite, from netlib public-domain or BSD code, and from the APIs of the fleet libraries. A reference is cited only once it has been opened. The go-numerics roadmaps cite R source lines that their authors read to understand an algorithm. This plan cites those roadmaps as fleet documents only and never follows their R line numbers.
data.contract-a-stated-bound-not-bit-identity:
The fleet rule (2026-11-11) applies: bit identity with R is a porting step, never the goal. Each slice states an error bound and the oracle that asserts it:
mpmath at 192 and 320 bits, stored as a double-double, for the special and distribution functions. This is the contract of go-numerics/special (docs/accuracy.md) and of go-statistics/stats (docs/accuracy.md); M4 adopts those budgets rather than inventing its own. special states them in its README “Accuracy contract” (go-numerics/special#69): per-region budgets of 1.5 times the measured maximum, and four BetaIncInv/BetaIncCInv regions (a or b < 1e-3) unbounded today (go-numerics/special#11). math/big for roots and minimisers (the root or minimum is recomputed at extended precision; the bound is on |x − x*| and on f). This is go-numerics/optimize’s contract (go-numerics/optimize#61: exact optima and a 300-bit math/big oracle, TestAccuracyBound… per solver family). mpmath quad at 50+ digits for quadrature (true error within the requested tolerance, and the reported error bounds the true error). R’s own value is always recorded beside ours in the golden. Where R is farther from the oracle than we are, the golden says so, and the difference is counted as an exclusion in the fuzz output, never hidden.
The one exception is the random streams (section 3): a seeded stream is a definition, not an approximation, so state equality is exact.

data.getting-the-oracle#Getting the oracle:
The tests that need R skip when Rscript is not found. To run them, install the pinned release, which conda-forge publishes for macOS arm64 and Linux x86-64, and point RGO_RSCRIPT at it:
micromamba create -y -p ~/r-4.6.2 -c conda-forge --override-channels r-base=4.6.2 export RGO_RSCRIPT=~/r-4.6.2/bin/Rscript RGO_REQUIRE_ORACLE=1 go test ./... # a missing R is a failure, not a skip go run ./cmd/roracle regen # rewrite testdata/golden RGO_REQUIRE_ORACLE=1 turns the skips into failures (CI sets it).
data.layout#Layout: Path Role rds/ R serialization reader and writer internal/oracle/ the driver of the reference R, and the R side of the protocol (oracle.R) internal/gen/ golden-file generators and readers cmd/roracle/ the command that regenerates the goldens testdata/ inputs written for this repository, and golden/
data.what-exists#What exists: internal/oracle starts one Rscript --vanilla process (the pinned release; any other version is refused at the greeting) and talks to it over stdin/stdout. Requests are R’s own serialization format, written by the Go rds package; replies are R serializations, one hex line each, so no JSON package is needed on the R side. Operations: eval, deparse, parsedata (utils::getParseData), describe, reserialize. Output, warnings and the condition class and message are captured and returned; each request gets a fresh environment; a per-call timeout kills R; R_MAX_VSIZE bounds its vector heap. The test suite starts a fake R from its own test binary, so the protocol and every failure mode are tested without R. rds reads and writes R’s serialization format (XDR, versions 2 and 3, gzip or bzip2 compressed): vectors of every atomic type, lists, pairlists, calls, symbols, closures, environments (with sharing and cycles), namespace and package references, built-ins, external pointers, S4 objects and ALTREP objects (kept in serialized form; Altrep.Materialize expands the compact sequences, wrappers and deferred strings). A decoded value encodes back to the same bytes: attributes in order, the object and general-purpose bits, string encoding flags, NaN payloads (NA_real_ is a NaN). Byte-code and promises are refused. The decoder is built for untrusted input: size limit after decompression (decompression bombs are refused), nesting limit, every claimed length checked against the bytes left before allocating. It is fuzzed (FuzzDecode, corpus in rds/testdata/fuzz). Since go-embedded-r/r pull request 25, which shipped in v0.10.0 (the tag at c1e0bd8 came after pull requests 25 and 26 were merged), an ALTREP object found in a version-2 stream is expanded, as R’s reader does (its ReadItem has no version test, while WriteItem emits ALTREP only for version 3 or later), so the decoded tree is always writable by the version-2 encoder; an unknown ALTREP class is a decode error, and the expansion is bounded by a cumulative budget of MaxBytes/8 elements. Version 3 is unchanged. cmd/roracle regenerates the golden files (roracle regen), prints the identity of the R that answers (roracle version) and evaluates a snippet (roracle eval 'expr'). Goldens (testdata/golden): deparse.jsonl is parse + deparse of the snippets in testdata/snippets.R (the input of the M1 parser), and rds.jsonl is serialize() of the expressions of testdata/values.R. Both inputs are written for this repository. The tests replay the goldens without R: every value R serialized decodes, agrees with R’s typeof and length, and re-encodes to R’s exact bytes; values built in Go encode to the bytes R writes. With R, the live tests check that R reads Go’s bytes back unchanged and that regenerating the goldens reproduces the committed files.

The package is github.com/go-embedded-r/r/syntax; the parser was released in v0.1.0 and deparse completes M1 in v0.2.0 (see Deparse).
f, err := syntax.ParseAll(src) // or ParseAllLimits(src, syntax.Limits{MaxBytes, MaxDepth, MaxNodes}) names, err := syntax.TopLevelNames(cell) // names a cell assigns and reads lines := syntax.Deparse(f.Exprs[0], nil) // deparse(), one string per line
data.bounds#Bounds: Bytes, tree depth (also for chains such as a+a+a+..., built by a loop) and node count; R’s own 50-level context stack (contextstack overflow). Bomb tests (200 000-deep chains of every shape) assert a refusal under a memory limit.
data.errors#Errors: *syntax.Error has Line, Col and Message, and its text is the message parse() signals, byte for byte, source context and caret included. Limits give a *syntax.LimitError (wraps ErrLimit). The statements before an error are kept in the returned File.
data.known-gaps#Known gaps: The effect of #line directives on the line numbers of later errors; parse(file=) encoding options; an invalid UTF-8 input is parsed as R’s lexer does, and for such text R cannot produce parse data, so tokens are not compared.
data.numbers#Numbers: A decimal literal is computed in double precision, digit by digit with an explicit fused multiply-add (math.FMA), then scaled by a power of ten: what R does on macOS arm64, where long double is double and the compiler fuses 10*ans + digit. 150 000 random literals are identical to that R’s, bit for bit, and the result is the same on every platform. R on x86-64 Linux accumulates in 80-bit extended precision and can differ by one unit in the last place on literals of more than 15 digits (the CI oracle lane saw it on 1e300), and by up to 6 ulp on literals near the subnormal range (measured on R’s own tests/: 290 literals differ, at most by 6 ulp). The parser is deterministic and matches the 64-bit reference; the platform-dependent literals are in testdata/numbers.R, compared within 16 ulp and kept out of the goldens. One literal differs by more: 1.7976931348623157e308 (the largest double) is Inf in 64-bit-double R and in the Go parser, and is kept by 80-bit R. Hexadecimal literals follow R’s rule (0x1.8p1).
data.parity-with-r-462#Parity with R 4.6.2:
Judged by the oracle, never by expectations written by hand: go run ./cmd/rparity ... parses the same text with R and with Go and compares

data.speed#Speed: One core each, interleaved rounds, median of 11 after a warm-up round, 1-minute load 7.8 on an Apple M-series laptop: the 842 files of src/library that both parse (7.8 MB) take 0.214 s in Go (syntax.ParseAll, which also builds the source map and the token list) and 0.269 s in R’s parse(text =, keep.source = FALSE): Go/R = 0.80 (go run ./cmd/rparity bench DIR).
data.the-tree#The tree: R’s own shape: operators, if/for/{/[ and the rest are calls to a symbol; Function carries the formals; |> is rewritten as R does; -> is <- with the sides swapped; a string callee is a symbol. Every node has a Span (line, column and byte range). File.Tokens are the terminals of getParseData() (SYMBOL_FUNCTION_CALL, SYMBOL_SUB, EQ_FORMALS, COMMENT, LINE_DIRECTIVE…).
data.toplevelnames#TopLevelNames: Assigned: <-, =, ->, "x" <-, f(x) <-, x$a <- (assign x), assign("lit", ...), for variables. Read: free variables and called names not bound earlier in the cell, under R scoping (function parameters and locals, local(); a function body may use anything the cell assigns anywhere). Dynamic (with Reasons) when names cannot be resolved: <<-, assign/get with a computed name or another environment, eval, parse, source, attach, library, require, sys.function, environment<-, load, list2env…

Since v0.6.0 (pull request 11, 2026-11-06), R’s regular expressions are TRE. The matcher is github.com/go-embedded-r/tre v0.1.0 (see The tre module), a Go port of TRE, the engine R uses for its default patterns (perl = FALSE, fixed = FALSE). It replaces the approximation on Go’s regexp of v0.5.0, whose lazy quantifiers, capture priority in repeated groups and \</\> differed from R.
grepl, grep, sub, gsub, regexpr, gregexpr, regmatches and strsplit use it. Lazy quantifiers, capture priority in repeated groups, back-references ((a)\\1, run by TRE’s backtracking matcher) and \< \> behave as in R. R’s choice of byte mode for all-ASCII input and wide mode otherwise is reproduced, with its quirks: an error text without the pattern for grepl and regexpr in wide mode, and the empty-match tokens of strsplit.
data.judged-by-r#Judged by R: Check Result R-level differential fuzz: random POSIX extended patterns, with lazy quantifiers, back-references, \< \> \b and non-ASCII text, through grepl, sub, gsub, regexpr, gregexpr, strsplit, regmatches (--mode regex; seeds 1, 7, 21; each function reported on its own line; nothing excluded) 60 000 / 60 000 goldens of testdata/eval, including regular expressions, against R 4.6.2 7 025 / 7 025 (v0.28.0) The port itself is also checked against upstream TRE; see The tre module.
data.memory-bounded-on-every-target#Memory: b: tre’s README has a “Limits and memory” section: the compile limits (MaxPattern 65 536, MaxNodes 2^17, MaxStates and MaxTransitions 2^19, MaxSetItems 2^17, MaxSteps 2^28) and a lazy DFA capped at 2 048 states. Measured peaks: every bomb test stays under 256 MiB on every target, wasm included, asserted by the tests; the whole bomb suite peaks at 124 MiB under wazero. Before tre v0.1.3 the deep-nesting pattern took 3.5 GiB. See The tre module.
data.related-limits-of-slice-3#Related limits: sort of non-atomic values is not implemented. sort and ls follow R’s ICU collation for Latin text since v0.7.0 (see M3 plan / base coverage).
data.rs-own-tre-behind-rcompat#R’s own TRE, b: R 4.6.2 ships a modified copy of TRE. The port’s Options.RCompat reproduces the behaviours where that copy differs from upstream ({,n}, bound overflow, the backtracking restart test, shared bracket positions, negated classes in copies of a repetition), so that go-embedded-r/r answers like R. They were found by diffing R’s copy against upstream, used as a specification only: no R source is copied, and the behaviours are judged by R itself.
data.speed-an-open-defect#Speed: an open defe:
grepl is 1.44 times slower than R 4.6.2 (Go time over R time), measured when tre v0.1.0 shipped: load 5.3, 5 interleaved rounds, one core, 20 000 lines. By the fleet rule, slower than the reference is an open defect: go-embedded-r/tre issue 3. The other cases of the same table: gsub with a class 0.87, gsub with a group 1.13 (also above 1), regexpr 0.92, back-references 0.99.
tre v0.1.1 (2026-11-07, pull request 7) adds a lazily built DFA for yes/no matches, used when no assertion depends on the position, and a start-position skip in the backtracker. Engine level, go test -bench, 20 000 lines, Apple M4: the grepl case [0-9]+@host[0-9]+\.example went from 5.95 ms to 0.69 ms; a back-reference case from 7.6 ms to 7.2 ms; the engines of regexpr and gsub with a group are unchanged. The end-to-end ratio against R has not been measured since: the machine’s load was far above the measuring limit of 8, so the tool refused. Issue 3 stays open until the table is measured at load 8 or below; the 1.44 above is the last measured figure.
go-embedded-r/r v0.7.1 also streams the loop of sub and gsub around the engine (matches are streamed, the replacement is parsed once, texts without a match ask the engine only for a yes/no, sub stops at its first match): BenchmarkGsubGroup, 20 000 lines, 247k to 87k allocations per operation and 9.0 to 4.6 MB per operation. Allocation counts are exact; no timing against R is claimed, because the load was above the measuring limit.
data.what-still-differs#What still differs: Approximate matching ({~1}, {+n}): the syntax is not ported and is an error. Non-ASCII classes follow Go’s Unicode tables, not a C library’s iswctype, so classes of non-ASCII characters can differ from R’s. perl = TRUE (PCRE) is refused: the call stops with an error that says it is not supported. Exponential backtracking is refused by a step limit, not run to the end. Some other pathological patterns are refused by limits too (pattern size, AST nodes, NFA states). useBytes and the multibyte-locale narrow API are not modelled. Patterns beyond the compile limits are refused (tre v0.1.3, in go-embedded-r/r v0.8.1): nesting thousands deep, huge repetition expansion, more than about 2^17 nodes. The call stops with regular expression '...' is too large for this evaluator (the engine’s ErrESpace). No golden or fuzz case reaches these limits, but R compiles some of those patterns, so some extreme patterns R accepts are now refused.

data:
github.com/go-embedded-r/tre (v0.1.0, 2026-11-06, pull request 1) is a pure-Go port of TRE, the POSIX regular expression engine (leftmost-longest, submatch addressing with tags, lazy quantifiers, back-references, \< \> \b \w \d \s, (?i) and friends) that R uses for its default patterns. It is what go-embedded-r/r runs since v0.6.0.
re, err := tre.Compile(`(a|ab)(c|bcd)(d*)`, tre.Extended) m, err := re.ExecString("abcd", 4, 0) // []tre.Match{{0,4},{0,1},{1,4},{4,4}} Offsets are in characters (UTF-8 decoded), or bytes with tre.UseBytes.
data.how-it-is-checked#How it is checked: TRE’s own tests: upstream’s tests/retest.c is run through a recording wrapper and replayed against the port: 286 compilations and 3514 executions (wide) and 3510 (narrow) with byte-for-byte equal return codes and match offsets. Excluded and counted: the 4 narrow-API patterns of retest’s EUC-JP section (20 executions), which run in a multibyte locale the port does not have. Differential fuzz against upstream TRE built as C: 197,588 compared, 0 mismatches. Excluded and counted: 2,410 approximate-matching patterns, 1 backtracking case cut by the step limit. R 4.6.2 for the R-level behaviour, through the regex fuzz of go-embedded-r/r (60 000 / 60 000, see Regular expressions). A fuzz target, bomb tests that assert refusals under GOMEMLIMIT and ulimit -v, govulncheck, 3 OSes with -race, 386, every GOOS, wasm.
data.licence#Licence: BSD 2-Clause, with the TRE notice kept in the repository’s NOTICE file. It is ported from upstream TRE at commit 71bfcaf (lib/tre-parse.c, tre-compile.c, tre-match-parallel.c, tre-match-backtrack.c, regexec.c): parse, AST, tagged NFA, the parallel matcher, and the backtracking matcher used only when the pattern has back-references.
data.limits-and-memory#Limits and memory:
A hostile pattern or subject gets an error (ErrESpace, ErrSteps), never an out-of-memory or a hang. The limits (pull request 10 documents them in the README):
Limit Default Bounds MaxPattern 65 536 pattern length in code units MaxNodes 2^17 AST nodes, including bounded-repetition copies MaxStates 2^19 NFA positions MaxTransitions 2^19 NFA transitions MaxSetItems 2^17 firstpos/lastpos entries, and the parent lists of nested groups MaxSteps 2^28 work of one match (ErrSteps); mainly for back-references The lazy DFA that answers yes/no matches is capped too: at most 2 048 DFA states and 2^18 NFA-state entries over all of them (about 2 MiB). At either cap it is switched off for that regexp and the NFA matcher answers, with the same result.
A pattern over a limit is refused with ErrESpace. This includes some patterns that R accepts: very deep group nesting (thousands of levels) and very large repetition expansions such as ((a{255}){255}){255}.
Memory guarantee. Measured peaks (the Go runtime’s Sys high-water mark over the bomb tests; nested counts, quadratic sets, 30 000 nested groups, a 2^20-state DFA, exponential back-reference backtracking): every bomb stays under 256 MiB on every target, wasm included, asserted by the tests (peak_test.go). The whole bomb suite peaks at 124 MiB under wazero, and the DFA bomb alone at 17 MiB natively. Before v0.1.3 the deep-nesting pattern took 3.5 GiB.
data.not-ported-and-open-issues#Not ported, a: Approximate matching ({~n}, {+n}, {1i+1d<2}): a pattern using it fails with ErrApprox. The C library’s system-wctype, multibyte-string and user-string front ends: one engine over []rune code units replaces them. Character classes use Go’s unicode tables, so classes of non-ASCII characters can differ from a given C library’s iswctype. Open: issue 3, grepl is 1.44 times slower than R 4.6.2; issue 4, upstream TRE reads one byte past the pattern in tre_regncompb.
data.rcompat#RCompat:
Options.RCompat reproduces the behaviours of R 4.6.2’s modified copy of TRE where they differ from upstream, so that go-embedded-r/r answers like R:
{,n} keeps a minimum of -1, so it matches n+1 repetitions (^a{,3}$ matches aaaa); a bound that overflows an int means “unbounded, or 1”; a bound above 255 is “Invalid contents of {}”; {m,n} expands to (|x(|x)) rather than (x(x)?)?. An empty REG_LITERAL pattern matches the empty string. The backtracking matcher decides whether to retry from a later start position by the current character instead of the character at the start of the attempt: ([abc]+)\w*\1 does not match banana in R. The items of a bracket expression (and the two cases of an (?i) literal) share one NFA position. tre_copy_ast forgets the negated classes of a copied literal: in wide mode [^[:space:]]{1,3} matches a space on its repetitions. Messages and limits: no TRE_MAX_RE, no REG_BADMAX, assert becomes an R error, one extra text for tre_version. R’s changes are GPL and were used as specification only; the behaviours are re-implemented and judged by R itself.

Engine-level grepl case: 5.95 ms to 0.69 ms on 20 000 lines. The speed ratio against R is not yet measured (load too high); issue 3 stays open.
